title: Research
text:
Published



International Evidence on the Relationship Between Financial Literacy and Corporate Cash Holdings

Download full paper


Yung, K., Kahibavil, R., Li, S., & Amidi, A. (2026). Journal of Corporate Accounting & Finance. Open access.


This study is the first investigation of the relationship between corporate cash holdings and financial literacy (FL). We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in FL is associated with an 8%–27% reduction in corporate cash holdings, depending on the measure of FL used. Moreover, higher FL reduces the market value of excess cash, indicating that financially literate environments discourage value-destroying cash accumulation. The results remain robust across alternative definitions of FL and cash holdings, estimation methods, and country subsamples. We further rule out the influence of endogeneity, refinancing risk, and variation in cash needs. Additional analyses identify agency costs as the primary channel through which FL affects corporate liquidity policies. The evidence suggests that financial literacy mitigates the agency motive for holding cash and serves as an effective substitute for monitoring opportunistic firm behavior when formal country governance structures are weak.

title: Research
text:
Accepted for conference & under review



Do Retail Investors Drive Lottery-Like Stock Mispricing?

Download full paper


Haghighi Zadeh, R., & Kahibavil, R. — accepted for presentation, Southern Finance Association Annual Meeting, 2026; under review, Journal of Banking & Finance. Preprint on SSRN.


This paper studies whether retail participation explains the underperformance of lottery-like stocks. Prior research links retail trading to attention-driven buying after salient events. In contrast, we examine systematic retail participation. Using weekly Robinhood holdings data, we construct measures capturing persistent ownership and flow dynamics rather than short-lived attention shocks. We study their relation to the MAX anomaly, the negative relation between extreme returns and future returns. Systematic retail participation predicts positive future returns, while the MAX anomaly remains negative and economically significant. Retail participation does not strengthen the MAX effect, indicating distinct sources of return predictability.





Expected vs. Unexpected Extremes: The Origins of the MAX Anomaly

Download full paper


Haghighi Zadeh, R., Kahibavil, R., & Safari, N. — accepted for presentation, Southern Finance Association Annual Meeting, 2026; under review, Review of Finance.


We find that the MAX anomaly is driven by unexpected extremes consistent with temporary mispricing rather than by predictable exposure to tail risk. Using daily returns for NYSE, Amex, and Nasdaq stocks from 1962 to 2023, we forecast next-month maximum daily returns using AR(1), ARMA(1,1), quantile–tail, and EVT-based models; the ARMA(1,1) specification provides the most accurate out-of-sample forecasts. Decomposing realized MAX into expected and unexpected components, portfolio sorts and Fama–MacBeth regressions show that expected MAX has little predictive power for future returns once unexpected extremes are considered, while stocks experiencing unexpectedly large extreme returns earn significantly lower subsequent returns. Double-sort analyses show that the strongest underperformance occurs when extreme realizations substantially exceed prior expectations, highlighting the central role of unexpected shocks in driving the MAX anomaly.

title: Research
text:
Working papers



Revisiting Cross-Listing: Examining Stock Returns and Market Integration

Download full paper


Kahibavil, R.


This study revisits the impact of cross-listing on major U.S. exchanges on financial integration, stock returns, and risk profiles of international firms, and investigates the return reactions of peers and the strategic adaptations they undertake in response to cross-listing. Using institutional and competitive dynamics theories, the research explores how enhanced legitimacy, reduced information asymmetry, and peer signaling affect firms’ financial outcomes post-cross-listing. The sample includes 1,142 cross-listed firms from 44 countries from 1990 to 2023. Employing event study methodology, the findings reveal that cross-listing lowers firms’ cost of capital, resulting in reduced expected returns and negative abnormal returns in the short and medium term after the announcement. Firms from non-segmented markets benefit more from cross-listing. Peer effects show that the cross-listing of a firm influences the abnormal returns of its peers, who adjust their strategies to compete more effectively within the newly integrated market environment.





Myopia, Investment, Innovation, and Stock Returns



Cohen, A. H., Kahibavil, R., & Zhang, W. — early draft


We examine whether national short-termism, inferred from corporate language, predicts subsequent real activity and equity market performance across countries. Using large-scale textual analysis of firm-quarter disclosures from the largest firms in the twenty largest equity markets, we construct a country-quarter Short-Termism Score (STS) capturing the relative emphasis on short-horizon versus long-horizon corporate language. Higher STS predicts lower subsequent capital formation and R&D intensity, and forecasts lower future equity index returns — indicating that aggregate managerial language carries forward-looking information about long-run value creation that is priced in national equity markets.
